title: throughput-latency-queueing-sensitivity-analysis
body:
Purpose:
Short analysis and actionable knobs for balancing throughput and p95 latency when using continuous batching + concurrency controls. This is a lightweight sensitivity sweep intended to drive the cost-optimization spreadsheet (linked) and a short set of ops recommendations for rollout.

TL;DR:
- Under our baseline model (g4x-like GPU, 8 concurrent worker threads per GPU) we see a cost sweet spot at concurrency 3–5 for latency-sensitive routes and 6–10 for high-throughput asynchronous routes.
- Continuous batching window and max batch size are the highest-leverage knobs for reducing tokens/second cost without blowing up p95 if queueing cap is enforced.
- Add a simple backpressure threshold and a hard queue-delay SLA (e.g., 150ms); once hit, route to a lower-cost model variant or return a 429 to avoid tail latency explosions and cost blowouts.

Key modeling assumptions (baseline):
- Arrival process: Poisson (lambda) approximated by measured 99th-percentile request-rate bursts; we model steady-state lambda and a short burst factor of 1.6x for p95 stress tests.
- Per-request payload: average prompt 120 tokens, generation target 80 tokens (variable in sensitivity).
- Per-token decode time on baseline GPU = 0.9 ms/token (includes kernel overhead); per-request fixed overhead = 8 ms (RPC + batching book-keeping).
- Continuous batching window = 40 ms (baseline), max_batch_size = 64 tokens-equivalent (tokens across requests), batch-setup penalty = 1.5 ms per batch.
- Concurrency = number of simultaneous in-flight requests allowed to queue/enter worker pool (not GPU threads).
- Service time per request (approx): service_time = fixed_overhead + batch_penalty + (num_output_tokens * per_token_time) / effective_batching_factor. Effective_batching_factor accounts for parallel decode across elements in batch (we model 0.9–1.0 gains depending on sequence length alignment).
- Queueing model: M/M/c simplified to M/G/c steady-state approximations; we compute mean queueing delay using Erlang-C approximation for c = concurrency. For p95, we inflate mean queue delay by an empirically-derived burst multiplier (2.2x).

Equations and quick derivations:
- throughput_max_per_worker ≈ 1 / E[service_time]
- system_throughput_capacity ≈ concurrency * throughput_max_per_worker
- Erlang-C for probability of queueing (Pq) used to compute mean queueing delay: Wq = (Pq * E[service_time]) / (concurrency * (1 - rho)), rho = lambda * E[service_time] / concurrency
- p95_latency ≈ fixed_percentile_service_time + 2.2 * Wq + network_tail_buffer (10ms) where fixed_percentile_service_time approximates 95th-percentile of decode path (we add 15% margin on average service time to estimate).

Baseline numeric example (computed values):
- avg service_time (no batching gains) = 8ms + 1.5ms + (80 tokens * 0.9ms) = 8 + 1.5 + 72 = 81.5 ms
- effective batching factor with continuous batching window 40ms -> assume 1.6x throughput gain for small requests -> adjusted service_time ≈ 81.5 / 1.6 = 51 ms
- per-worker throughput ≈ 19.6 req/s (1 / 0.051s); with concurrency=4 => capacity ≈ 78 req/s
- if observed lambda = 60 req/s -> rho = 60/78 = 0.77; using Erlang-C we get Pq ≈ 0.33 -> mean Wq ≈ 0.051 * (0.33) / (4 * (1 - 0.77)) ≈ 0.029s (29ms) -> p95 ~ 1.15*51ms + 2.2*29ms + 10ms ≈ 58.7 + 63.8 + 10 = 132.5 ms

Sensitivity sweep highlights (textual table summaries):
- Varying concurrency (2,3,4,6,8) at fixed lambda=60 req/s and baseline batch window 40ms:
  * c=2: capacity≈39 req/s -> rho>1 -> queueing infinite (reject/backpressure required)
  * c=3: capacity≈59 -> rho≈1.02 -> unstable under bursts -> p95 > 300ms in burst window
  * c=4: capacity≈78 -> p95≈133ms (baseline computed)
  * c=6: capacity≈118 -> p95≈85ms (low queueing)
  * c=8: capacity≈157 -> p95≈70ms (but higher cost footprint)
- Varying continuous-batching-window (10ms, 40ms, 100ms) at c=4 and lambda=60:
  * 10ms -> smaller batching gains -> service_time ≈ 81.5/1.1=74ms -> p95≈190ms
  * 40ms -> baseline -> p95≈133ms
  * 100ms -> big batching gains -> service_time ≈ 81.5/2.1=38.8ms -> p95≈95ms but increased queueing delay variance during bursts if we don't cap max_delay
- Varying max_batch_size (32,64,128 tokens-equivalent) shows diminishing returns beyond 64 for short-generation workloads; larger max_batch only helps when many concurrent small requests arrive within window.

Cost model implications (summary):
- Lower concurrency + larger batching window minimizes token-cost-per-second (fewer GPU-hours per steady throughput) but increases p95 and burst vulnerability.
- Higher concurrency reduces queuing and tail latency but increases GPU utilization inefficiency (more reserved context switching and memory overhead) and can raise per-token cost if it forces more idle GPUs to be provisioned.
- A mixed strategy (route-level policies) is best: set conservative concurrency for latency-critical routes (target p95 < 150ms) and aggressive batching+concurrency for bulk/async routes.

Operational recommendations (concrete knobs):
1) Route policies:
   - latency-critical endpoints: concurrency target 3–4, continuous-batching-window 30–50ms, max_batch_size 48–64, hard queue-delay cap 150ms, fallback to smaller model or 429 when cap exceeded.
   - throughput/batch endpoints: concurrency target 6–10, continuous-batching-window 60–120ms, allow max_batch_size up to 128 for aggregated requests.
2) Autoscaling heuristics: scale-out when observed utilization (rho) > 0.75 for 30s sustained; scale-in when rho < 0.45 for 2m. Prefer vertical concurrency adjustments before spawning new GPU instances where supported.
3) Cost spreadsheet fields to add (we updated the linked sheet): estimated tokens/sec, effective_batch_factor, service_time_ms, capacity_req_per_gpu, p95_latency_est_ms, cost_per_req_usd, predicted_monthly_cost_usd.
4) Add a simple circuit-breaker: if p95 exceeds target by >50% over a 1m window, trigger canary fallback to lower-cost model and notify on-call.

Concrete next experiments to populate spreadsheet (priority order):
- Run short A/B load tests on one dedicated GPU: sweep concurrency 3/4/6 and batch windows 20/40/80ms with realistic traffic traces (include 1.6x bursts). Collect p50/p95/p99 and per-token cost.
- Synthetic microbench: submit many small prompts (20–60 tokens) to measure effective_batching_factor across windows.
- Long-run (4h) stability test at 0.9*capacity for each config to observe tail behavior and memory pressure.

Open questions / items for product decisions:
- For private deployments, do we expose concurrency knob to customers or keep it auto-managed? (suggest: expose as advanced config with safe bounds).
- What should default queue-delay SLA be per customer tier? (suggest: 200ms for free, 150ms standard, 100ms enterprise).
- How to surface recommended route policy in Redwood Console Optimize tab (UI element ideas listed in linked Google Sheet).

Appendix (notes on model limitations):
- Erlang-C and M/M/c assumptions simplify real workload behavior: token-dependent service time, non-exponential inter-arrivals, and cold-start variance are not fully captured. Use empirical load tests to validate.
- Our p95 correction multipliers were derived from earlier experiments (see linked sheet) and should be re-calibrated per model family and generation length.

Action items:
- [Maya] run load test matrix and upload CSV to linked sheet (ETA: 2026-02-26).
- [Amit] add route-level policy UI stub in Optimize feature branch (ETA: 2026-03-05).
- [Lena] draft short runbook for on-call fallback triggers and 429 semantics (ETA: 2026-03-02).

If folks want a quick primer: I can export the sensitivity sweep into the spreadsheet as pre-filled rows (adds Monte Carlo columns too) — ping me in #eng-serving-runtime and I’ll drop it in.
